khawaja_claims.title: Sandpaper was used at Port Elizabeth
khawaja_claims.proposition: Sandpaper was discussed and used on the match ball at Port Elizabeth, before the Cape Town exposure.

basis.text: Brettig’s November 7 report attributes this earlier onset to Khawaja’s book, locating first use on day two. In the ABC interview Khawaja stands by what he saw and the conversations he had at Port Elizabeth.
basis.limit: The newspaper contains a reporter’s summary of the book, not the complete first-person chapter. Khawaja’s reported 2018 notes are not in the archive.

supporting.title: Two other participants describe direct involvement
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft describes taking sandpaper onto the field after tea on day two and using it. Sayers places his first awareness at Port Elizabeth and describes sandpaper being handed to him to take off the field. Those accounts support actual use and handling, beyond an inference from reverse swing.
supporting.limit: These are distinct participant accounts, but all emerged publicly years later. Their independence in every detail is not established. Sayers assumes, rather than distinctly recalls, who handed it to him.

challenging.title: The contemporary first-occasion account conflicts with the new chronology
challenging.reasoning: Smith’s immediate March 2018 press conference presented the incident as the first occasion under his leadership. That is a contemporaneous account against the later onset narrative.
challenging.limit: CA later charged Smith with misleading public comments. Contemporaneity alone does not make that account reliable. Cummins’s lack of earlier knowledge also cannot prove that earlier use never occurred.

challenging.title: Agreement on onset does not establish continued use
challenging.reasoning: Bancroft describes continued use through Port Elizabeth and Cape Town; Sayers qualifies his belief that it was not used again in that Port Elizabeth Test. This prevents treating their accounts as mutually confirming every part of the chronology.
challenging.limit: Sayers’s limited recollection is not a categorical observation of non-use. This disagreement bears on duration more than on their common account of an earlier start.

khawaja_claims.assessment: Earlier onset has comparatively substantial participant support in this record. It remains a retrospective account without captured contemporary physical or broadcast confirmation. Duration is more disputed than onset.
unresolved: Do the reported 2018 notes record the timing, and can their provenance be established?
Which innings and sessions involved actual use, removal or reuse?
Is there contemporary footage or an independently recorded observation of the Port Elizabeth use?

khawaja_claims.title: Knowledge extended beyond the three sanctioned players
khawaja_claims.proposition: More than Smith, Warner and Bancroft knew about sandpaper use before it became public.
khawaja_claims.kind: Factual knowledge: at least one additional person

basis.text: Khawaja’s original interview says the team knew and should respond together. This narrower proposition follows from his broader allegation; it is not a substitute for assessing his claim that everyone knew.
basis.limit: Define the match and the knowledge claimed: awareness of actual use is different from knowledge of a particular future implementation plan.

supporting.title: Sayers admits his own knowledge and handling
supporting.reasoning: If Sayers’s account of knowing about sandpaper and helping remove it is true, at least one additional squad member knew. That establishes a narrower proposition without first proving what each frontline bowler knew. Khawaja also places himself beside Bancroft and asserts awareness of relevant events.
supporting.limit: Sayers’s Port Elizabeth involvement does not by itself establish knowledge of a particular Cape Town plan. His further inference about everyone is a separate claim.

challenging.title: The official finding was explicitly confined to three
challenging.reasoning: CA’s public finding said prior knowledge of the Cape Town incident was confined to Smith, Warner and Bancroft. That is a materially conflicting institutional account.
challenging.limit: The underlying report and witness evidence are unavailable here. Its incident-specific scope cannot settle every act on the tour, and later first-person admissions must be assessed rather than excluded merely because they conflict with it.

khawaja_claims.assessment: Wider-than-three knowledge has a stronger affirmative case than universal knowledge, especially through Sayers’s self-admission. A failure to prove that everyone knew would not establish that only three knew.
unresolved: Who knew of sandpaper specifically, at which match and before which event?
How does the official finding’s precise remit relate to the later Port Elizabeth admissions?
What did Khawaja personally hear, see or say before the exposure?

khawaja_claims.title: “All of us”: every player and staff member knew
khawaja_claims.proposition: All players and staff knew about sandpaper use before the Cape Town screen footage.

basis.text:
Khawaja’s original newspaper interview expressly includes batters, bowlers and staff in his all-of-us account. The proposition tested here is that every relevant player and staff member knew about sandpaper use before its public exposure. Knowledge of reverse swing, knowledge of a proposal, knowledge of actual use and participation in cheating are distinct. Someone could know and object.

The [individual Cummins question](/questions/cummins-in-2018/) examines his evidence separately; this page compares the three witnesses across the whole group.
basis.limit: The complete Sabr chapter and reported 2018 notes are absent. The November 7 article mixes direct interview quotations with Brettig’s book summaries; the ABC transcript preserves Khawaja’s answers separately from Ferguson’s premises. Bancroft’s later specificity cannot be inserted into Khawaja’s account. The captured Bancroft statement is a bylined access copy, not an independently compared original; direct listening checks for the interviews remain open.

supporting.title: Khawaja: reported dressing-room observations, without individual bowler particulars
supporting.reasoning:
**What the captured sources say he saw or heard.** Brettig’s account of the book describes open Port Elizabeth discussion about roughing the ball and sandpaper, Smith distancing himself, and Bancroft volunteering. At Cape Town it places Khawaja beside Bancroft, observing an exchange with an unnamed coach. ABC’s later live blog also reports a book scene involving a dressing-room sandpaper demonstration and laughter, and quotes an unnamed coach asking Bancroft to do more. Those are attributed book accounts, not the complete chapter or independent witnesses to the scenes.

**Who he specifically identifies.** In the November 7 reported scenes, Smith and Bancroft are named; the coach is not. The captured material does not give Khawaja’s person-by-person account of Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood or Lyon acknowledging sandpaper. His broader language implicates the whole group, including himself, but it is less specific than Bancroft’s subsequent account.

**What he says directly when pressed.** Khawaja stands by what he saw and the conversations at Port Elizabeth, says he deliberately removed names, and declines to answer whether the named bowlers participated in discussions or Cummins knew. Ferguson supplies the categorical inference about Cummins; Khawaja does not expressly confirm it.
supporting.limit: His broad assertion is affirmative testimony and should not be erased by the non-answer. But the non-answer supplies no additional named observation. His reported proximity could make him a useful witness to a coach’s exchange; proximity alone does not show that every nearby person heard it. The reported 2018 notes are not contemporary corroboration until their actual contents and provenance can be examined.

supporting.title: Bancroft: named exchanges, an alleged open acknowledgment, and an informed instruction
supporting.reasoning:
**At the Port Elizabeth tea break.** Bancroft says Warner proposed sandpaper and explained why camera attention meant he could not use it himself. He puts Saker and Lehmann in the conversation, recalls people agreeing, and says Smith entered and distanced himself. He expressly qualifies this: not everyone was in the room, and he cannot speak for every word shared.

**On the field.** He admits using sandpaper and names **Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh** in conversations about whether the ball was reversing enough. He names **Paine** as another source of feedback, recalls more work being requested and a warning to stop, and singles out Marsh joking about the swing. At Cape Town he says exchanges continued with those four fast bowlers, Paine and unnamed slips fielders. He explicitly alleges that these teammates knew he was using sandpaper, rather than merely working the seam; that allegation must be preserved.

**The strongest alleged disclosure to a group.** He says that at the usual team chat on the morning of Port Elizabeth day three, his sandpaper use the previous evening was discussed and acknowledged. He singles out **Saker’s** encouragement and **Kate Hutchison’s** objection and departure. This is a much more direct proposed route to shared knowledge than the proposition that all bowlers must notice a ball’s condition. Hutchison is described as objecting, not approving.

**At Cape Town.** He names **Saker** as the coach who instructed him to do more with sandpaper. He also places himself beside Khawaja and Paine. His later story about **Handscomb and Lehmann’s radio instruction** is expressly after he was caught; it is evidence of alleged knowledge then, not by itself before exposure.
supporting.limit: This is the most specific witness account in the three, but it is retrospective. Bancroft admits earlier withholding of material facts and says Khawaja’s book revived memories. His explicit knowledge allegation goes beyond the mostly swing-related words he recounts to bowlers; a competing innocent interpretation remains possible unless context establishes shared knowledge. The alleged day-three discussion is more probative if accurately recalled, but the archive lacks an attendance list or another comparably detailed account of that meeting. A vivid memory is not independent verification.

supporting.title: Sayers: direct knowledge and handling; broader knowledge asserted partly by inference
supporting.reasoning:
**What he says he personally knew and recalls.** Sayers locates his first knowledge at Port Elizabeth and remembers numerous dressing-room conversations about reversing the ball and what would be used. He does not remember whose idea it was. He says he recalls Bancroft agreeing to act and explains Warner’s non-participation by camera attention; he does not supply a direct Warner quotation proving the origin of the plan.

**His physical involvement.** He says sandpaper was handed to him to take off the field while he brought drinks. He assumes Bancroft passed it, rather than distinctly recalling the handover person, and cannot remember what he did with it afterwards. If accepted, his own admitted knowledge and handling are powerful evidence of an additional informed squad member.

**Who else he identifies.** Bancroft and Warner appear in his account of the plan. He does not name a frontline bowler’s sandpaper acknowledgment or an individual coach’s instruction in this interview. Asked whether the frontline bowlers could have been unaware, he reasons that a reverse-swing effort requires everyone to buy in and concludes everyone knew. His confidence is broader than the named observations he supplies.
supporting.limit: Sayers is not merely repeating Khawaja: he alleges personal knowledge and handling. But that is stronger proof about Sayers than about every other person. He does not recall discussion of the strategy’s success when asked, and believes use did not continue in that Port Elizabeth Test; Bancroft says it continued. Their agreement on onset and wider awareness is not agreement on duration or independent corroboration of Bancroft’s next-morning meeting.

challenging.title: Cummins: an explicit personal denial, with an alternative reading of the feedback
challenging.reasoning:
**Against which allegation?** Bancroft names Cummins in feedback conversations at both Tests and says the bowlers knew the method. Khawaja’s group allegation includes him, but the captured Khawaja answers do not give a specific Cummins acknowledgment.

**The captured response.** On November 13 Cummins says he did not know sandpaper was going onto the field and that the earlier Port Elizabeth episode was news to him. He also rejects being an architect of a sandpaper scheme. On the reported dressing-room demonstration, he has no recollection but expressly does not say it never happened. On the coach’s demand for more and a bowler’s instruction to stop further ball work, he lacks specific recollection but says such feedback could happen. He offers routine ball management as an explanation for swing-related language.

**How it stacks up.** His knowledge denial directly conflicts with Bancroft’s asserted shared understanding. His alternative account does address the ambiguity of feedback about swing. It does not refute a correctly recalled open discussion naming sandpaper. Rejecting authorship of a scheme is also a stronger denial than rejecting mere awareness; proof of one would not automatically prove the other.

**After Bancroft spoke.** In the [November 19 ABC report](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-19/pat-cummins-maintains-position-on-sandpapergate/107402100), Cummins’s manager Neil Maxwell reaffirms the unchanged position and says the earlier conference answered Bancroft’s allegations. That is a response after the statement, conveyed through his manager; it does not add a new detailed recollection of each disputed exchange.
challenging.limit: The November 13 conference predates Bancroft’s November 18 statement. The later endorsement through Maxwell should not be omitted, but does not turn the earlier answers into a new passage-by-passage interview. His denial is participant testimony, not independent exoneration; qualified recollections must not be upgraded into categorical denials of events.

challenging.title: Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon: distinguish the named exchanges from the group denial
challenging.reasoning:
**Starc.** Bancroft names him in feedback exchanges at both Tests. Starc’s November 10 response reiterates that he did not know a substance was taken onto the field before the Cape Town screen footage. The same report says he knew nothing of the newly alleged Port Elizabeth use. The latter is reporter-attributed rather than a separately printed direct quotation. This is relevant beyond the Cape Town-only framing, although he also says he has not read the book.

**Hazlewood.** Bancroft names him in the same exchanges. His captured denial is the joint 2021 statement, rather than a separate response to the detailed 2026 account.

**Lyon.** He signed the 2021 statement, but is not one of the four fast bowlers Bancroft names in these feedback passages. The universal group allegation includes him; these passages do not narrate a Lyon-specific exchange.

**The joint statement.** Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon deny knowing a foreign substance had been taken onto the field until the big-screen images. The statement frames the dispute around Cape Town and does not separately discuss the newly alleged Port Elizabeth episode. That is a scope distinction, not proof of what they knew at Port Elizabeth.
challenging.limit: The captured denials conflict with asserted prior knowledge but cannot settle it independently. Neither an older denial nor the absence of a newer individual reply resolves a specific later allegation. Mitchell Marsh is not a signatory. Do not put Greenberg’s separate remarks in the Starc article into Starc’s mouth.

challenging.title: Saker: the sharpest named coaching conflict
challenging.reasoning:
**The allegation.** Bancroft names Saker in the Port Elizabeth proposal discussion, in next-morning encouragement of acknowledged sandpaper use, and as the coach instructing him to do more at Cape Town. Khawaja’s captured book reports leave that coach unnamed.

**The captured denial.** In June 2021 Saker expressly says he had no idea sandpaper was involved and understood the methods to be normal reverse-swing tactics.

**How it stacks up.** This is a direct substantive conflict over Saker’s knowledge. Bancroft alleges informed involvement, not mere presence. The exact words reported from Khawaja’s book about doing more do not themselves name the material, so their context matters; Bancroft’s later assertion supplies the explicit sandpaper link.
challenging.limit: The older Saker denial predates these specific allegations. His May 2021 broad-blame remarks do not concede sandpaper knowledge, and a full older conference would not automatically answer the later named account. No specific later Saker reply is captured here.

challenging.title: Lehmann: alleged presence versus a personal knowledge denial
challenging.reasoning:
**The allegation.** Bancroft places Lehmann in the Port Elizabeth sandpaper discussion, while qualifying what he can say about every word shared. He also attributes a radio instruction to Lehmann after the Cape Town exposure.

**The captured denial.** ABC’s November 7 report says Lehmann denies personal sandpaper knowledge and rejects assuming the entire camp knew. His official 2018 resignation statement also expressly denies prior knowledge.

**How it stacks up.** His presence as Bancroft recalls it gives a concrete reason to ask what he heard; it does not by itself establish hearing or understanding the proposal. The after-exposure radio story cannot establish pre-exposure knowledge without an additional link.

**After the detailed statement.** The [November 19 ABC report](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-19/pat-cummins-maintains-position-on-sandpapergate/107402100) says Lehmann wanted time to process the allegations and work through them before commenting. That is not yet a substantive answer to each later particular.
challenging.limit: His lack of recollection about a later collective-responsibility meeting is a different issue and is not a denial that every earlier conversation occurred. The November 7 response predates Bancroft’s detailed statement.

challenging.title: Hick: an explicit denial with no individual contrary episode in these accounts
challenging.reasoning:
**The allegation.** Khawaja’s universal staff wording includes Hick. None of the specific passages examined from Khawaja, Bancroft and Sayers names an instruction by Hick or a particular sandpaper conversation he heard. Bancroft’s general references to coaching staff do not supply an individual attendance record.

**The captured denial.** Hick’s November 11 response says he did not hear or know of tampering discussions at Port Elizabeth or Cape Town and first learned of it from the screen footage while on the balcony.

**How it stacks up.** If true, Hick’s account defeats a literal everyone-knew claim. It would not establish that only three knew, or disprove another coach’s participation. The present affirmative case against Hick is broad inclusion, rather than a matching named observation.
challenging.limit: The archive has the four substantial quoted paragraphs in a published report, not a separate authored original or recording. The denial remains his account, not independently established fact.

challenging.title: Paine: named feedback, but his older memoir is not a complete denial of the later particulars
challenging.reasoning:
**The allegation.** Bancroft names Paine as giving feedback from behind the stumps at Port Elizabeth and Cape Town, and places him beside Bancroft and Khawaja at Newlands.

**The captured account.** Paine’s published 2022 memoir passages describe shock at the screen images, reject the inference that everyone in a dressing room must know everything, and deny a team meeting planning what to do to the ball. They also express regret that the team did not own the affair together and describe ordinary ball-management instructions.

**How it stacks up.** The privacy and ball-management explanations challenge automatic knowledge from proximity or feedback. But shock at exposure is not logically identical to prior ignorance, and the quoted passages do not separately answer Bancroft’s later named exchanges. Regret about collective ownership is not an admission of sandpaper knowledge.
challenging.limit: The 2022 excerpts predate the specific 2026 account. The denial of a planning meeting must not be stretched to cover every informal conversation, a different next-morning discussion or a post-exposure responsibility meeting. Sitting beside an exchange is not proof of hearing it.

challenging.title: Marsh, Hutchison and Handscomb: three different limits on implication
challenging.reasoning:
**Mitchell Marsh.** Bancroft names him in feedback exchanges and jokes about swing. Marsh’s captured November 12 refusal to share his account is neither an admission nor a denial, predates Bancroft’s statement and does not answer those later particulars. He did not sign the four-bowler statement.

**Kate Hutchison.** Bancroft alleges a specific objection to sandpaper at the day-three team discussion and a later conversation about the consequences of being caught. If accurate, that supports awareness and opposition, rather than complicity. Her own account is not captured. It would be a particularly useful test of whether the alleged open discussion happened.

**Peter Handscomb.** Bancroft’s named account of his involvement is explicitly after exposure. It therefore does not, by itself, establish that Handscomb knew beforehand. The same timing limit applies to the radio instruction attributed to Lehmann.
challenging.limit: Do not use refusal, missing testimony or post-exposure action to fill a pre-exposure knowledge gap. Do not conflate Mitchell with Shaun Marsh, or imply Hutchison approved what she is alleged to have opposed.

challenging.title: The official finding and ball inspection do not resolve the person-by-person conflict
challenging.reasoning:
CA’s public finding confines prior knowledge of the Cape Town incident to Smith, Warner and Bancroft and assigns particular acts to them. It is an institutional account against wider knowledge, but its underlying report and interview evidence are not available here. The finding does not establish a person-by-person answer to the newly alleged Port Elizabeth events.

The ICC independently records that umpires saw no marks warranting a ball change, while still finding attempted alteration. This weakens the claim that every bowler must have noticed visible damage. It does not answer an allegation of a prior conversation about sandpaper, and it concerns the inspected Cape Town ball, not every earlier ball.

Smith and Warner’s knowledge at Cape Town is already specified in the public charges; that is a baseline, not evidence that every additional person knew. Bancroft’s and Khawaja’s earlier Port Elizabeth scenes still need to be tested on their own evidence.
challenging.limit: An institutional conclusion is not a substitute for the missing underlying evidence; nor does a later contradictory statement make every new detail true. The visible-condition argument and the private-conversation argument require different answers.

khawaja_claims.assessment: The captured record contains direct self-implication by Sayers, Khawaja’s broad assertion and reported observations, and Bancroft’s much more specific allegations against named people. That makes wider-than-three knowledge a materially stronger case than universal knowledge. The strongest test of broad disclosure is Bancroft’s alleged Port Elizabeth day-three discussion explicitly about sandpaper, not the assumption that bowlers must know. The sharpest named coaching conflict is Saker; the bowlers’ swing feedback still admits a competing interpretation. Hick is included by the universal allegation without a named contrary episode in these passages. The denials remain live, and the captured record does not establish every individual’s pre-exposure knowledge. None of this turns shared knowledge into identical participation or blame.
unresolved: Who attended the alleged Port Elizabeth day-three discussion, what exact material was named, and what does each attendee independently recall? Hutchison’s own account could test both knowledge and objection.

For each named bowler and Paine, what words or circumstances establish that the feedback referred to sandpaper, rather than ordinary ball management? Bancroft asserts that link; which recollections independently confirm or contradict it?
What did Saker and Lehmann each hear or say, and is there a direct response to the specific later allegations rather than only an older general denial?
What specific observation places Hick or Lyon in an informed pre-exposure conversation? Broad inclusion and a roster are not individual evidence.
What do the complete Sabr chapter and reported 2018 notes actually say? Keep reporter summaries, opponent paraphrases and Ferguson’s premises distinct from Khawaja’s own detailed evidence.
How should the conflict about continued Port Elizabeth use affect confidence in the later recollections? Preserve Sayers’s qualifications rather than calling all three accounts identical.
Direct listening checks remain open. Published quotations are used here; no new exact-word or speaker-boundary certification is claimed.

khawaja_claims.title: A coach encouraged Bancroft to do more
khawaja_claims.proposition: A coach encouraged Bancroft’s activity during the Cape Town Test, contributing to the exposed sandpaper use.
khawaja_claims.kind: Specific event and alleged informed encouragement

basis.text: The November 7 report says an exchange with an unnamed coach helped set events off. ABC later reports the book’s words about doing more. This establishes the initiating Khawaja allegation without silently naming the coach for him.
basis.limit: The complete chapter is absent. These are attributed book summaries or selected quotations, rather than a captured full first-person narration.

supporting.title: Bancroft later identifies Saker and the instruction
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft expressly names Saker as the coach who told him to do more at Cape Town. He separately alleges praise from Saker at Port Elizabeth. His specific account supports the claimed exchange more directly than generic talk of a permissive culture.
supporting.limit: The Port Elizabeth praise is a different event. The later testimony is retrospective and does not independently authenticate every word of Khawaja’s earlier account.

challenging.title: The words require a link to sandpaper knowledge
challenging.reasoning: An instruction to do more of whatever is making the ball swing could encourage activity without showing knowledge of the material. Saker’s explicit 2021 sandpaper-knowledge denial conflicts with informed encouragement if the instruction involved known sandpaper. His broad-blame comments do not concede that link.
challenging.limit: The older denial predates the specific allegation. Cummins’s lack of recollection and Lehmann’s unawareness are not eyewitness refutations. Hick’s personal denial does not establish what another coach said.

khawaja_claims.assessment: There is specific additional participant support for the exchange; the speaker’s knowledge and exact context remain decisive. General cultural responsibility, encouragement and knowing sandpaper instruction carry different burdens.
unresolved: What did the coach understand Bancroft to be doing when speaking?
Who else heard the exchange, and what happened immediately before it?
Is there a direct response to this specific 2026 allegation? A full older conference is useful context, not automatically an answer.

khawaja_claims.title: Smith heard the earlier discussion and distanced himself
khawaja_claims.proposition: At Port Elizabeth Smith heard the sandpaper discussion and distanced himself rather than stopping it.

basis.text: Brettig summarises the book as describing an open Port Elizabeth discussion and Smith signalling that he did not want to know.
basis.limit: This is reporter narration of the memoir, not a verbatim captured statement by Smith or the complete chapter.

supporting.title: Bancroft recalls a similar response
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft says Smith entered the conversation and distanced himself, and recalls a further similar response during the match. Separately, CA’s charges identify Smith’s knowledge of a potential plan and failure to prevent it at Cape Town.
supporting.limit: The CA charge supports Cape Town knowledge and failure to prevent, not independent corroboration of the earlier Port Elizabeth date or remembered words.

challenging.title: Distancing does not settle either authorship or adequate intervention
challenging.reasoning: The later accounts distinguish Smith’s response from the proposal and instructions attributed to Warner. Wanting no part in a plan need not mean authorising it, while a captain’s withdrawal need not discharge a duty to stop it.
challenging.limit: This is a limit on the inference, not a captured denial that the earlier conversation occurred. The archive has no complete contemporary record of Smith’s Port Elizabeth response.

khawaja_claims.assessment: Cape Town knowledge and failure to prevent are specified in CA’s public charges. The earlier exchange has later participant support but remains unverified against a contemporary record. Neither operational authorship nor effective intervention follows from distancing alone.
unresolved: What exactly did Smith hear, understand, say and do at Port Elizabeth?
Were any instructions to stop given or enforced?
Which parts of the alleged response concern Port Elizabeth, and which concern Cape Town?

khawaja_claims.title: Khawaja tried to delay the immediate press conference
khawaja_claims.proposition: After the exposure, Khawaja urged Smith not to rush into the post-play press conference with Bancroft.

basis.text: The original report attributes this intervention to Khawaja’s book.
basis.limit: The report’s view that the conference worsened the scandal is retrospective narration. The attempt to delay it and the predicted benefit of delay are separate claims.

supporting.title: Bancroft also recalls disagreement about speaking immediately
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft remembers some people wanting to wait until the following day and Smith wanting to address the matter immediately. That is consistent with a disagreement about timing.
supporting.limit: These passages do not identify Khawaja as the person urging delay. They corroborate the general disagreement rather than every part of his account.

challenging.title: The precise intervention and its benefit remain unverified
challenging.reasoning: The captured accounts do not establish the exact alternative Khawaja proposed or show that a delay would have produced a more truthful or less damaging statement. Bancroft’s separate allegation about coordinating a false material explanation is an additional claim.
challenging.limit: There is no captured named denial of Khawaja’s intervention. An absence of contemporary confirmation must not be presented as affirmative contrary testimony.

khawaja_claims.assessment: Partly consistent later testimony supports a timing disagreement. Khawaja’s specific role has limited corroboration; any claim that waiting would have improved the outcome is counterfactual.
unresolved: Who proposed waiting, and what did they propose saying instead?
Was the purpose to obtain facts, legal advice, a common account or something else?

khawaja_claims.title: Khawaja urged a shared response after exposure
khawaja_claims.proposition: Khawaja advocated collective responsibility in a dressing-room meeting after the scandal became public.

basis.text: In the original interview Khawaja recounts asking the team to take responsibility together after the game. His ABC answers reiterate that stance.
basis.limit: The existence and content of a proposal must be separated from whether it was right and whether it would have changed sanctions.

supporting.title: Other accounts recall discussions about the response
supporting.reasoning: Sayers recalls a lengthy discussion after that day’s play and, when prompted, vaguely remembers resistance by two players. Bancroft describes a lengthy players-and-staff meeting after the match about the public response.
supporting.limit: The after-day and after-match accounts may describe different meetings. Sayers does not name the objectors. Bancroft’s description does not independently establish every word of Khawaja’s proposal.

challenging.title: Cummins cannot recall the proposed collective response
challenging.reasoning: Cummins says he does not remember a conversation about collective responsibility or Khawaja standing up to advocate it. Lehmann neither confirms nor denies the meeting, referring to multiple rooms and meetings and his contact with CA.
challenging.limit: Failure to remember is weaker than a categorical denial. Paine’s 2022 denial of a prospective planning meeting concerns what the team would do to the ball, not necessarily a later meeting about responsibility.

khawaja_claims.assessment: There is affirmative testimony for a proposal and partial support for response meetings, but the chronology, attendance and exact proposal remain unresolved. Neither general regret nor a denial about a different meeting settles this event.
unresolved: Which meeting, on which day, is each witness recalling?
Was the proposal a common factual confession, a shared public statement, equal penalties or support for the three?
Who heard it, how did they respond, and is any contemporaneous record available?

khawaja_claims.title: The investigation missed relevant witnesses
khawaja_claims.proposition: The 2018 investigation was rushed or incomplete and failed to seek Khawaja’s relevant evidence.

basis.text: Khawaja says he was not interviewed despite sitting beside Bancroft. He calls the process insufficiently thorough and rushed. The original report also describes time pressure and a Cape Town focus.
basis.limit: His non-interview is a first-person factual claim; the quality of the whole investigation is a broader judgment. The reporter’s account of remit is not the underlying terms of reference.

supporting.title: Other relevant evidence may also have been missed or withheld
supporting.reasoning: Sayers says he expected an interview and was not interviewed despite his own claimed involvement. Bancroft admits omitting material timing and knowledge information from the process. These are concrete reasons to question exhaustiveness.
supporting.limit: They do not establish the full witness list or prove investigators knowingly suppressed evidence. Bancroft’s concealment could contribute to an incomplete result without institutional intent.

challenging.title: CA describes a thorough process; other participants were interviewed
challenging.reasoning: The public releases defend the investigation’s thoroughness. Cummins says he was interviewed and recalls requests for other information. Saker also describes participating. These accounts show an investigative process, rather than no inquiry.
challenging.limit: They do not explain the alleged omissions or establish that every relevant witness was sought. An invitation to volunteer is not automatically sufficient investigation of an obvious witness.

khawaja_claims.assessment: The claimed non-interviews raise a substantial procedural question. The completeness judgment cannot be settled from public assurances or later recollections alone; remit, witness selection and treatment of conflicting evidence matter.
unresolved: What were the exact remit, witness list, interview questions and evidentiary standards?
Why were Khawaja and Sayers allegedly not approached?
What opportunities to volunteer evidence existed, and what was actually supplied?

khawaja_claims.title: Khawaja alleges deliberate exclusion from the inquiry
khawaja_claims.proposition: Khawaja was deliberately not interviewed because investigators knew he wanted collective responsibility and would tell the truth.
khawaja_claims.kind: Intent and causal motive, expressed as belief

basis.text: In the original November 7 interview Khawaja explicitly says he feels this was why he was not interviewed. The later ABC answer stops short of calling the process a cover-up and describes it as rushed.
basis.limit: Both statements belong in the record. The later qualification must not erase the stronger original motive allegation; the original belief must not become an established finding.

supporting.title: His claimed proximity, stance and omission make the suspicion concrete
supporting.reasoning: Khawaja says he sat beside Bancroft, advocated a shared response and waited for an interview that never came. Sayers alleges another potentially relevant non-interview. Those facts, if accepted, are compatible with selective avoidance.
supporting.limit: Compatibility is not proof of motive. No cited witness supplies investigator communications explaining a decision to avoid inconvenient testimony.

challenging.title: The record does not discriminate between deliberate avoidance and other explanations
challenging.reasoning: Haste, a narrow remit, reliance on incomplete answers or poor witness selection could also produce omissions. Bancroft admits withholding facts. Khawaja’s later cover-up qualification itself limits how firmly he puts the intentional-concealment case.
challenging.limit: These alternatives are possible explanations, not established excuses. CA’s general assurances do not independently resolve intent either. Sayers’s speculation about reasons cannot supply the missing investigator evidence.

khawaja_claims.assessment: This serious intentional-act allegation has much thinner support than the non-interview claim. The archive has circumstantial suspicion, not evidence establishing why investigators selected or omitted witnesses.
unresolved: Who selected witnesses, and what did they know of Khawaja’s stance?
Is there a contemporary record explaining why he was not interviewed?
What evidence would distinguish a flawed or hurried inquiry from deliberate avoidance?

khawaja_claims.title: The group should have shared accountability
khawaja_claims.proposition: The team and institution should have shared accountability instead of leaving the central burden on three players.

basis.text: Khawaja frames his intervention as justice for the sanctioned three and says the team should have owned what happened together.
basis.limit: This is a moral claim with factual premises. Wider cultural responsibility, knowing participation, equal blame and equal sanctions are different propositions.

supporting.title: Wider participation and institutional culture support a wider response
supporting.reasoning: If more people knowingly participated, a three-person factual account is incomplete. Separately, the Ethics Centre assigns responsibility for cultural failure to CA; Lehmann accepts responsibility for team culture while denying prior knowledge. Paine later regrets the team’s limited support and wonders whether joint ownership would have helped.
supporting.limit: The cultural review is not a reinvestigation proving every person knew about sandpaper. Shared moral regret does not prove a specific meeting or instruction occurred.

challenging.title: Specific individual acts still warrant differentiated responsibility
challenging.reasoning: CA differentiates Smith’s knowledge and failure to prevent, Warner’s development and instructions, and Bancroft’s implementation and concealment. A common benefit or failed culture does not erase those acts. Nor were the three the only people to face any consequence: Lehmann resigned and CA underwent a cultural review.
challenging.limit: Those wider consequences do not settle their adequacy or whether the three bore a disproportionate burden. Khawaja does not demand identical bans; the moral remedy needs to be specified.

khawaja_claims.assessment: Broader cultural responsibility has substantial institutional and participant support. What justice required beyond it remains a reasoned moral judgment: acknowledgement, differentiated sanctions, institutional change and personal support need separate consideration.
unresolved: What should a shared account have admitted about each person’s conduct?
What form of responsibility is sought: public acknowledgement, sanction, institutional reform or support?
How should responsibility reflect knowledge, power, action and opportunity to intervene?

khawaja_claims.title: A shared response would have changed the bans
khawaja_claims.proposition: If the team had owned the incident together, the whole team would not have been banned and the three would not have borne the same sanctions alone.

basis.text: Khawaja says the three bans were inappropriate and he does not believe the whole team would have been banned had they gone in together, reasoning that banning an entire team would be difficult.
basis.limit: This is his predicted alternative, not a historical decision. It is not a demand for identical punishment for everyone.

supporting.title: Other participants question the severity and value of individualising the response
supporting.reasoning: Paine thinks collective ownership might have worked out better for the three. Cummins regards their punishment as excessive. The ICC sanctions were substantially lower than CA’s, providing a concrete proportionality comparison.
supporting.limit: The ICC and CA applied different codes and remits. Agreement that sanctions were excessive does not establish what CA would have done after a different admission.

challenging.title: No alternative decision or controlling reason establishes the predicted outcome
challenging.reasoning: CA justified sanctions by integrity and reputational harm. A shared statement could have widened exposure, changed the evidence or left the individual charges intact. The archive contains no alternative disciplinary ruling showing that team ownership would prevent or reduce bans.
challenging.limit: That makes the prediction untested, not impossible. The specific admissions, applicable powers and complete reasons would be needed to assess it properly.

khawaja_claims.assessment: A plausible but untested counterfactual. The proportionality dispute has concrete comparative material; the prediction about a whole-team response is materially less established.
unresolved: What exactly would a joint statement have admitted?
Under the applicable 2018 codes, who could be charged for which conduct?
Would collective ownership have altered evidence, penalties, public support or all three?

khawaja_claims.title: Ball manipulation and a win-at-all-costs culture preceded the scandal
khawaja_claims.proposition: Ball manipulation was normalised in Khawaja’s Australian teams and competitive pressure helped create the conditions for sandpaper use.

basis.text: Khawaja describes earlier ball-working methods and says sandpaper was new on that South African tour. Brettig summarises the book’s account of competitive pressure. Khawaja also reports what he heard about South Africa from another player.
basis.limit: The other-team claim is hearsay. His experience of Australian teams is not knowledge of every team everywhere. His characterisation of methods as prohibited is not an independent historical rules ruling.

supporting.title: Several accounts and the cultural review support a broader problem
supporting.reasoning: Paine’s 2022 interview describes widespread tampering and excessive competitive culture. Lehmann discusses broad ball-tampering practices while distinguishing individual knowledge. The Ethics Centre identifies institutional cultural failures.
supporting.limit: Convergence about culture does not prove the same incident, method, legality or individual awareness. It can explain conditions without excusing deliberate acts.

challenging.title: Permitted management and prohibited alteration must not be collapsed
challenging.reasoning: Cummins describes the team’s intended methods as legal; Saker denies condoning cheating. Those positions require examining the actual method and governing rules rather than assuming all work on a ball is equivalent.
challenging.limit: They do not establish that every method was lawful or disprove a specific illegal act. The disputed automatic legal/illegal wording remains open; this analysis uses the published report and makes no new ruling under 2018 law.

khawaja_claims.assessment: There is substantial convergence on a broader cultural problem. The legality and causal role of each practice still require event-specific evidence and the applicable historical rule. Culture alone cannot decide who knew of sandpaper.
unresolved: Which practices occurred, when, and under which exact rule?
How did competitive pressure affect specific decisions rather than merely accompany them?
What distinguishes tolerated methods, concealed violations and the sandpaper escalation?

khawaja_claims.title: The scandal still hangs over Bancroft
khawaja_claims.proposition: Bancroft continues to carry career and reputational harm despite strong domestic performances.
khawaja_claims.kind: Continuing harm; distinct from a proven selection veto

basis.text: Khawaja says Bancroft has not regained his place despite scoring runs and that the scandal hangs over him. He presents this as part of the injustice to the three.
basis.limit: This does not itself allege a specific bowler veto or establish a causal explanation for every selection decision.

supporting.title: Bancroft describes continuing concern, and selectors acknowledge his runs
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft’s later account expresses concern about dressing-room tensions and missed opportunities. Bailey’s account acknowledges excellent Shield performance and a difficult 2024 selection decision. This makes Khawaja’s concern concrete rather than resting on no sporting case.
supporting.limit: Bancroft’s selection suspicions are his later account, not a more specific allegation that can silently be attributed to Khawaja. Strong output alone cannot identify a selector’s motive.

challenging.title: The 2024 selector gives competing cricketing reasons
challenging.reasoning: Bailey denies a political or bowler veto and explains the preference for Green in the best six, Smith opening and Renshaw next in line. Bancroft himself acknowledges poor-form periods and competing candidates.
challenging.limit: This is the selector’s stated account, not an independent audit; it addresses a particular selection window, not every later opportunity or the full extent of stigma.

khawaja_claims.assessment: Continuing stigma has firsthand support. A stronger claim that the scandal caused a particular non-selection remains decision-specific and weakly established by runs or suspicion alone.
unresolved: Which selection window and role are being challenged?
What were the alternatives, fitness considerations and contemporaneous reasons?
What evidence could separate reputational stigma from a causal selection exclusion?

khawaja_claims.title: What evidence did Khawaja give that race cost him the Test captaincy?
khawaja_claims.proposition: In Sabr, Khawaja identified race as the more important reason he believed he was passed over for the interim Test captaincy in 2018.

basis.text: Khawaja gave two reasons for being passed over. He identified his role in the 2017 pay dispute and gave greater weight to the selectors’ readiness to appoint a brown Australian captain.
basis.limit: AAP reproduces the relevant passage. The archive has not acquired the complete chapter.

supporting.title: The chairman’s reported assessment
supporting.reasoning: Khawaja said the chairman had told a journalist he knew that Khawaja lacked the qualities sought in a captain. Khawaja took the remark to refer to his background and skin colour.
supporting.limit: The quoted remark contains no reference to race. The racial explanation comes from Khawaja.

challenging.title: Khawaja’s answer on evidence and Cummins’s response
challenging.reasoning: Khawaja acknowledged the lack of concrete evidence when Ferguson asked. He said he could never be certain and thought in hindsight that Paine was the right choice. Cummins rejected the suggestion that skin colour could exclude someone from the job and called for evidence.
challenging.limit: The selectors’ actual reasons remain unconfirmed by these accounts.

khawaja_claims.assessment: Khawaja attributed the decision to race in his book. The chairman’s reported remark questioned his suitability for the job. Khawaja supplied the racial interpretation and later acknowledged he had no concrete evidence for it.
unresolved: What did the chairman mean by his reported assessment of Khawaja, and what reasons did the selectors give when they chose Paine?

analysis_status: Source-linked archive analysis; no prescribed verdict

claims.title: Was sandpaper used before Cape Town?
claims.proposition: Sandpaper was used on the match ball in the second Test at Port Elizabeth, before the televised Cape Town incident.
claims.scope: The relevant event is actual match use at Port Elizabeth. Sandpaper in a kit bag, practice on a training ball, and ordinary ball maintenance are different propositions.

supporting.title: Khawaja’s original report alleges the earlier start
supporting.reasoning: The November 7 report attributes Port Elizabeth discussion and use to Khawaja’s book; he later stands by what he saw and the conversations he had there. This is the initiating allegation, distinct from Bancroft’s later details.
supporting.limit: The newspaper’s event sequence is reporter narration of the memoir, not the acquired chapter. The reported 2018 notes are not captured or authenticated.

supporting.title: Bancroft supplies a first-person account of using it
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft describes taking sandpaper onto the field after tea on day two and using it when he collected the ball. He describes repeated use and feedback during the session. If accurate, this directly supports earlier use rather than merely a plan.
supporting.limit: This is a 2026 recollection. Bancroft says his 2018 account omitted when the practice began; contemporary corroboration is still needed.

supporting.title: Sayers describes a separate physical involvement
supporting.reasoning: Sayers places his first awareness at Port Elizabeth and says sandpaper was handed to him to take off the field. That is a potentially corroborating act by another participant, beyond a general belief that everyone knew.
supporting.limit: He says he assumes Bancroft handed it to him, cannot remember what he did with it afterwards, and qualifies his belief that it was not used again in that Port Elizabeth Test. Bancroft separately describes continuous use through the rest of that Test and Cape Town. Agreement on onset does not independently corroborate duration; preserve the disagreement and uncertainty.

challenging.title: The contemporary public account said this was the first occasion
challenging.reasoning: Smith told the March 2018 press conference this was the first time under his leadership. That is a contemporary account in tension with the later Port Elizabeth accounts.
challenging.limit: Its reliability is itself disputed: CA subsequently charged Smith with misleading public comments. A contemporary statement is not automatically a truthful one.

challenging.title: Cummins says the Port Elizabeth allegation was new to him
challenging.reasoning: The captured Cummins coverage records his denial of knowing about sandpaper use at Port Elizabeth. It challenges the claim that the practice was common knowledge.
challenging.limit: Lack of knowledge is not direct observation that the act never occurred. This is a challenge to shared knowledge, with less force against the narrower proposition that Bancroft used it.

unresolved: Obtain and compare contemporary footage, any physical evidence and other first-person accounts specific to Port Elizabeth.
Resolve Sayers’ limited recollection about when the sandpaper was removed and whether use continued.
Do not infer the success or frequency of tampering from the number of wickets alone.

claims.title: Who knew, and when?
claims.proposition: Members of the bowling group knew about sandpaper being used on the match ball before the Cape Town television footage exposed it.
claims.scope: Assess each person and occasion separately. Knowing the ball was reversing, suspecting alteration, knowing sandpaper was being used, and directing its use are distinct claims.

supporting.title: Bancroft names the bowlers and connects their feedback to his actions
supporting.reasoning: He recalls conversations with Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh, says he used more sandpaper in response to feedback, and describes those exchanges continuing at Cape Town. This is more specific than an unnamed claim that the whole team knew.
supporting.limit: He also acknowledges that knowledge of reverse swing, suspicion of alteration and knowledge of sandpaper differ. Feedback about swing alone cannot independently prove the third proposition.

supporting.title: Sayers says his own awareness was wider than the punished trio
supporting.reasoning: Sayers describes knowing about planned use and helping remove sandpaper, then questions how the original finding could be limited to three. If his account is accurate, at least one additional squad member had knowledge.
supporting.limit: His further inference that every frontline bowler must have known is not a recollection of each person explicitly acknowledging it.

supporting.title: The 2021 interview shows the original question and hesitation
supporting.reasoning: In the complete published Guardian interview, McRae asks twice whether bowlers knew. Bancroft’s answers imply awareness while stopping short of naming a person or recounting a particular acknowledgment. This establishes an earlier public implication rather than one invented in 2026.
supporting.limit: The interviewer’s view that others must have known is editorial framing, not Bancroft’s testimony. His qualified and hesitant answer is weaker than an explicit account of who knew what.

supporting.title: Khawaja explicitly asserts wider knowledge in the original newspaper interview
supporting.reasoning: The published interview attributes to Khawaja an all-of-us account and quotes his insistence that the team knew and should take responsibility together. This is affirmative evidence of his stated position, alongside the later ABC interview in which he declines to identify named bowlers.
supporting.limit: Collective wording does not provide an individual account of when each person learned of sandpaper. The complete memoir chapter and any underlying contemporaneous notes are not captured. The article’s summaries of book events must not be treated as the full chapter.

challenging.title: The four bowlers directly denied prior knowledge
challenging.reasoning: The 2021 joint statement says they did not know a foreign substance had been taken onto the field until the big-screen images. Cummins repeated a personal denial in 2026.
challenging.limit: These are the participants’ denials, not an independent finding that settles the later conflicting testimony. The four signatories do not include Mitchell Marsh. In his 12 November 2026 response, Marsh declines to share his account or explain the non-signature. That refusal is neither a denial nor an admission and predates Bancroft’s later detailed statement.

challenging.title: Handling the ball or sharing a dressing room does not make awareness inevitable
challenging.reasoning: The bowlers point to the umpires finding no visible reason to replace the ball. The ICC’s contemporary release independently records that inspection result. This challenges the argument that the alteration must have been obvious to everyone handling it. Paine’s published 2022 memoir passages separately reject the inference that everybody in a dressing room must know, saying players and staff keep things to themselves.
challenging.limit: An umpire’s inability to see damage does not establish anyone’s private knowledge, and it concerns the inspected Cape Town ball rather than every earlier ball. Paine’s general objection predates the detailed 2026 allegations and does not independently refute Bancroft’s named conversations.

challenging.title: Scope limit: Khawaja declines to confirm named bowlers’ knowledge
challenging.reasoning: In the full ABC interview, Ferguson repeatedly asks about named bowlers and specifically Cummins. Khawaja declines to answer and says he deliberately avoided names, while advocating collective accountability. The interview therefore cannot be presented as a specific factual confirmation that each named bowler knew. This limits the specificity of the evidence; it is not affirmative testimony against the claim.
challenging.limit: Declining to answer is not a retraction or proof of ignorance. The complete memoir chapter is still needed to assess the factual observations he asks readers to consider.

challenging.title: Starc repeats a personal denial rather than supplying a different full-team account
challenging.reasoning: The captured November 2026 report quotes Starc saying his recollection is unchanged and that he was unaware of a substance being taken onto the field before seeing it on the big screen. It adds a contemporaneous personal response to the 2021 joint denial.
challenging.limit: The full press exchange is not captured, and the quoted denial concerns his knowledge; it cannot independently establish what others knew. The report also says he had not read the book.

challenging.title: Cummins offers a different explanation of the huddle language
challenging.reasoning: ABC’s live record captures the specific question about telling teammates not to do anything else to a reversing ball. Cummins says he does not remember that exchange but describes similar instructions as part of ordinary ball maintenance. This is a competing explanation for feedback that the wider-knowledge argument treats as incriminating.
challenging.limit: This is his explanation of normal practice, not independent proof of what happened in that huddle or a historical ruling that every method he describes was lawful. Lack of recollection is not proof the conversation did not happen.

unresolved: For each named person, what direct words or actions establish specific knowledge before exposure?
Which accounts concern Port Elizabeth and which concern Cape Town?
Can the original investigation interview records or contemporaneous communications resolve the conflicting accounts?

claims.title: Did coaches know or encourage it?
claims.proposition: At least one member of the coaching staff knew about or encouraged match-ball tampering with sandpaper before it was publicly exposed.
claims.scope: Presence at a discussion, knowing of the plan, encouraging it and learning of it after the television exposure are different propositions. A claim about one coach does not establish the knowledge of all staff.

supporting.title: Khawaja’s account alleges an exchange with an unnamed coach
supporting.reasoning: Brettig’s book summary says a coaching exchange helped set off the Cape Town events. ABC later reports the book’s selected words asking Bancroft to do more. Bancroft’s later statement names Saker; that identification must not be put into Khawaja’s mouth.
supporting.limit: The complete chapter is missing. An instruction to do more is not by itself proof that the speaker knew sandpaper was involved; its context must supply that link.

supporting.title: Bancroft identifies a coach and a specific instruction
supporting.reasoning: He identifies Saker as the coach who told him to do more during the Cape Town innings and recalls playing and coaching staff acknowledging his work at Port Elizabeth. These are allegations of prior encouragement, not merely awareness afterwards.
supporting.limit: These are later allegations. Saker’s May2021 broad-blame comments and June2021 explicit personal denial are both now collected; neither is a response to Bancroft’s specific2026 instruction allegation. His complete current response and direct corroboration are still needed.

supporting.title: The alleged discussion was wider than two players
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft says Saker and Lehmann were present as the sandpaper proposal developed and recalls people agreeing. He also describes Hutchison objecting to what was happening at a later team discussion.
supporting.limit: He expressly cannot speak for every word shared, says people moved in and out, and says Hutchison deserves her own account. Physical presence does not by itself establish knowledge or endorsement.

challenging.title: Smith’s original account excluded the coaches
challenging.reasoning: At the initial press conference Smith said the coaches were not involved and attributed the decision to the leadership group. This is a direct competing account of who participated.
challenging.limit: CA later charged him with misleading public comments about the nature and participants of the plan; the initial exclusion cannot be treated as independently verified.

challenging.title: Post-exposure instructions cannot alone prove earlier knowledge
challenging.reasoning: Bancroft recalls Handscomb relaying Lehmann’s instruction to remove the sandpaper after he had been caught and infers Lehmann must already have known. The timing also permits knowledge acquired from the newly exposed footage.
challenging.limit: This timing objection narrows the inference from that incident; it does not answer Bancroft’s separate allegations about earlier changing-room discussions.

challenging.title: Lehmann’s contemporary denial and later recollection both remain on record
challenging.reasoning: The newly collected official 2018 report reproduces Lehmann’s explicit denial of prior knowledge, omitted from the other published transcript in this archive. In ABC’s 2026 coverage he disputes universal knowledge; on the collective-responsibility meeting he says he does not remember and cannot confirm or deny it.
challenging.limit: The complete ABC episode and an automatic draft are now collected, but its exact wording is not listening-verified. General knowledge that ball tampering exists and acceptance of cultural responsibility are not admissions of knowing this sandpaper plan. A personal denial does not establish every coach’s knowledge.

challenging.title: Hick expressly denies knowing of discussions at either Test
challenging.reasoning: In his statement to the original newspaper, Hick says he did not hear or know of discussions about tampering at Port Elizabeth or Cape Town and first learned of it from the big-screen footage. This directly contests a literal claim that every staff member knew beforehand.
challenging.limit: The capture is the complete published report with his quoted statement, not a raw interview recording. His denial is a participant’s competing account; it does not independently settle other staff members’ knowledge.

challenging.title: Saker’s later 2021 response explicitly denies sandpaper knowledge
challenging.reasoning: The June3 report quotes Saker saying he had no idea sandpaper was involved and understood the team to be using normal reverse-swing tactics. That is an express personal denial, more specific than his May remarks about a monumental mistake and many people to blame. Both belong in the record.
challenging.limit: This is a contemporary publisher report with selected direct quotations, not the full underlying conference or verified audio. It predates the specific2026 allegations and does not establish another coach’s knowledge.

challenging.title: Saker’s 2019 public denial concerns condoning cheating
challenging.reasoning: In the original May 2019 interview report, Saker says the team had never condoned cheating. This is an earlier public denial relevant to the encouragement part of the claim, alongside his separate June 2021 denial of sandpaper knowledge.
challenging.limit: Not condoning, not knowing and preventing an incident are different propositions. The report contains selected interview quotations and predates the specific 2026 allegations; it does not establish what Saker privately knew or answer the later alleged instruction directly.

unresolved: Seek direct responses to the specific 2026 instructions where a real public source lead exists. The complete older Saker conference and Hick original are conditional context gaps, not automatic blockers; a longer Hick response is not assumed. Fuller Hutchison or Handscomb accounts matter if they test a specified conversation. Lehmann’s collected recordings still require exact-word listening verification.
What did each person hear before the cameras exposed the incident?
Do contemporary staff communications, audio or investigation records corroborate the alleged instructions?

claims.title: Who devised and directed the plan?
claims.proposition: Warner was a principal initiator of the sandpaper plan and instructed Bancroft to carry it out.
claims.scope: Warner’s involvement and whether it was exclusive are separate propositions. A team benefit or permissive culture does not by itself establish collective planning or absolve the person who proposed the method.

supporting.title: The public charges specifically attribute development and instruction to Warner
supporting.reasoning: CA’s published account charges Warner with developing the plan, instructing Bancroft and demonstrating how to alter the ball. The 2024 review decision records Warner accepting the report’s description of his conversation and demonstration.
supporting.limit: The 2024 proceeding concerned modification of a sanction, not a new investigation of everyone’s role. Acceptance of Warner’s involvement does not establish exclusivity.

supporting.title: Bancroft’s later account still identifies Warner’s proposal
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft says Warner raised sandpaper and explained why camera attention meant he could not carry it out personally. Even the account alleging wider involvement retains a concrete initiating role for Warner.
supporting.limit: Bancroft frames it as happening within wider team conversations; acknowledging the proposal is compatible with others’ encouragement or prior knowledge.

supporting.title: The complete Gilchrist interview directly names Warner
supporting.reasoning: Asked who requested the action, Bancroft says Warner suggested it. The question and answer supply a direct attribution from Bancroft in December 2018, before his more expansive 2026 account.
supporting.limit: The interview does not establish that Warner acted alone; it also records Bancroft’s choice and desire to fit in. Interview content must not be reduced to a headline assigning all responsibility to Warner.

challenging.title: Scope limit: wider participation does not refute Warner’s initiating role
challenging.reasoning: He recalls people agreeing, others offering views on when to act, and playing and coaching staff later acknowledging his role. If accurate, the organisational setting involved more than a private instruction between two players. This challenges exclusivity, not the proposition that Warner was a principal initiator.
challenging.limit: Participation in discussion and collective benefit must still be distinguished from authorship of the plan, express approval and knowledge in each case.

challenging.title: Corroboration limit: Sayers does not recall the origin
challenging.reasoning: Sayers remembers discussion and Bancroft agreeing to act, but explicitly says he does not remember whose idea it was initially. His account cannot independently confirm the origin of the proposal.
challenging.limit: Failure to remember an origin is not positive evidence that Warner did not propose it. It limits corroboration rather than refuting the specific allegation.

challenging.title: Erskine alleges wider instructions and protection of others
challenging.reasoning: Warner’s manager says more than three were involved, says he advised Warner to protect colleagues, and alleges earlier instructions by executives in Hobart. These claims raise a possible institutional context beyond a single player’s initiative.
challenging.limit: These remain a manager’s allegations, with no established basis that he witnessed the Hobart exchange. The executives are unnamed and a 2016 allegation does not itself establish a 2018 sandpaper instruction. Full audio and an automatic draft are now collected; the bowlers commentary after the guest farewell belongs to the host, not Erskine. Wider instructions would not themselves disprove Warner’s own initiating role.

unresolved: Compare the now-captured complete Gilchrist interview with the 2026 account, especially the distinction between suggesting the method and wider participation.
What does the original investigation evidence establish about proposal, agreement and demonstration separately?
Does anyone identify another initiator with direct rather than second-hand knowledge?

claims.title: What did Smith know and do?
claims.proposition: Smith knew about a potential sandpaper plan but distanced himself instead of authorising or directing its implementation.
claims.scope: Knowledge, failure to prevent, approval, concealment and misleading explanations are distinct forms of responsibility. A person can decline direct participation while still failing in a leadership duty.

supporting.title: The CA charges distinguish his role from Warner’s
supporting.reasoning: Smith’s charges concern knowledge of a potential plan and failure to prevent it, whereas Warner’s include development, instruction and demonstration. This is evidence that CA did not publish identical allegations against them.
supporting.limit: The same charge list also attributes concealment and misleading explanations to Smith. Different charges do not amount to exoneration or prove that he lacked authority to stop it.

supporting.title: Bancroft recalls Smith explicitly distancing himself
supporting.reasoning: Bancroft says Smith entered the Port Elizabeth discussion, wanted no part in it and distanced himself; he recalls a later similar response. This supports knowledge plus disengagement rather than direct physical implementation.
supporting.limit: It is a later recollection and does not establish whether the disengagement was a sufficient intervention or what Smith knew at each later stage.

challenging.title: Smith originally accepted a leadership-group decision
challenging.reasoning: His initial account described the leadership group’s idea and accepted responsibility. The ICC records his admission that he was party to a decision to attempt an unfair alteration.
challenging.limit: The initial public account was subsequently challenged as misleading. It is necessary to establish what he meant by leadership group rather than assume every senior player participated.

challenging.title: Distancing oneself does not answer prevention and concealment
challenging.reasoning: CA’s public charges include failure to prevent implementation, directing concealment and misleading officials and the public. Those allegations challenge a reading of disengagement as no meaningful involvement.
challenging.limit: The complete underlying investigation records are missing; the source establishes the public charge, not independent observation of each alleged act.

challenging.title: His full return-home statement accepts a failure of leadership
challenging.reasoning: Smith describes allowing it to happen, calls it a failure of his own leadership and declines to blame Warner. This counters an interpretation that a limited role meant no responsibility.
challenging.limit: Accepting leadership responsibility does not specify that he personally developed the sandpaper method or demonstrate every act alleged in the charges.

unresolved: Compare the now-captured original questions and answers with underlying investigation records when available; different admissions have different scopes.
What specific acts did Smith take to stop or facilitate the plan?
Separate judgments of captaincy responsibility from claims about physical tampering or devising the method.

claims.title: Was the public explanation coordinated?
claims.proposition: The inaccurate tape explanation and omission of wider involvement were coordinated beyond Smith and Bancroft.
claims.scope: That an explanation was inaccurate is different from who devised it, who knew it was false, who agreed and who later relied on it. An accusation of continuing coordination requires evidence beyond the original incorrect account.

supporting.title: The material explanation changed in an acknowledged way
supporting.reasoning: The initial public account describes tape and granules. Bancroft’s 2026 statement explicitly says sandpaper was concealed behind that explanation and calls it another lie. CA’s charges also identify misleading public comments.
supporting.limit: This strongly supports inaccuracy of the early account, but not by itself the identity or number of those who coordinated it.

supporting.title: Bancroft alleges specific advice before the press conference
supporting.reasoning: He identifies Saker as warning against naming sandpaper and says coaches, management and players discussed the response, with some agreeing and others disagreeing. This is an allegation of coordination beyond the two speakers.
supporting.limit: The account is retrospective and does not identify every participant or supply their exact responses. It needs the named staff responses and contemporaneous corroboration.

challenging.title: The early account does not itself identify a wider cover-up group
challenging.reasoning: Bancroft described panic when seen on the screen, while Smith publicly assigned the original plan to a leadership group and excluded coaches. Neither establishes who proposed the later tape story beyond the people who spoke.
challenging.limit: Panic and wider coordination can coexist; the early account’s failure to identify others is not proof others were uninvolved.

challenging.title: Silence at a post-exposure meeting does not establish earlier agreement
challenging.reasoning: Bancroft recalls nobody professing ignorance at the subsequent meeting and others advising how to minimise damage. By then sandpaper had been exposed; that silence cannot on its own establish prior knowledge or a prior pact.
challenging.limit: This challenges the inference from that meeting, rather than refuting the specific allegation of pre-conference advice.

unresolved: Verify the published original Q&A against recordings and obtain complete relevant staff accounts.
Which proposed statements were agreed before the first press conference, and by whom?
Treat later inconsistency, an admitted omission and a proven continuing agreement as different findings.

changes.description: The Cape Town Q&A gives tape and granules as the material and excludes coaching involvement.
Bancroft’s return-home Q&A explicitly acknowledges lying about sandpaper and says he panicked. The admission of the material lie did not first arrive in 2026.
The Gilchrist interview acknowledges the lie while discussing accountability and why the original conference happened immediately.
Bancroft supplies an allegation about pre-conference advice from Saker and others, adding alleged coordination beyond the already-acknowledged lie.

claims.title: Did the investigation settle who knew?
claims.proposition: The 2018 investigation’s public finding reliably establishes that only Smith, Warner and Bancroft had prior knowledge of the incident.
claims.scope: There is a published finding that prior knowledge was confined to three. Whether the available evidence justifies treating that finding as exhaustive is a separate question. Different reviews have different remits.

supporting.title: CA published a specific finding and individual charges
supporting.reasoning: The reproduced official release expressly confines prior knowledge to three and differentiates their conduct. In 2021 CA said its integrity unit asked Bancroft for new information and he supplied none.
supporting.limit: The underlying investigation report, interview schedule and complete evidence are not in this archive. An official conclusion and a later absence of supplied evidence are not substitutes for those records.

supporting.title: Participants say they answered the investigators’ questions
supporting.reasoning: The fuller ABC live record quotes Cummins saying he was interviewed, answered truthfully and recalls requests for anyone with different accounts or information to come forward. This is evidence of his participation and his stated account of the process. The June2021 Saker report also describes his interview and quotes his account of having taken part.
supporting.limit: His experience does not establish that every relevant witness was interviewed or that the investigators received all relevant information.

challenging.title: An alleged relevant witness says he was never interviewed
challenging.reasoning: Sayers describes helping remove sandpaper and says he expected an interview but was never interviewed. If accurate, his potentially relevant evidence was not directly tested in the original process.
challenging.limit: The publisher transcript prints a speculative suggestion about knowing too much. The recording’s automatic editions do not independently settle that exact verb phrase, and in any event it is not evidence of investigator motive. His stated non-interview and the reason for it are separate propositions.

challenging.title: Bancroft says he withheld material facts from investigators
challenging.reasoning: His later statement admits that he did not give a complete truthful account and omitted timing and others’ awareness. If accepted, this directly limits the information on which the original process could rely.
challenging.limit: An admission of earlier concealment also bears on evaluating his later credibility. It does not automatically make every new allegation true.

challenging.title: Khawaja alleges both an omission and a reason for it
challenging.reasoning: Khawaja’s original November 7 interview says he was not interviewed despite sitting beside Bancroft and explicitly alleges, as his belief, that investigators knew he wanted collective responsibility and would tell the truth. His later ABC answer describes a rushed process and stops short of calling it a cover-up. Both accounts must be preserved; non-interview, adequacy and intent are separate claims.
challenging.limit: The claimed omission raises a procedural question but does not establish investigator motive. No captured witness-selection record explains the decision. The stronger original allegation must not be erased by the later qualification or presented as proven by the omission.

unresolved: Obtain or establish the availability of the underlying report, interview list and contemporaneous witness accounts.
What new evidence, rather than repeated allegation, has each later account supplied?
